intro: Brzoza maps three trees protected in a single sentence of Polish municipal law: an oak and two limes standing within fifteen metres of each other in ordinary state forest north of Toruń. The Wielka Nieszawka council made all three nature monuments on the same day in 2014. None carries a documented age, and two rest on a single source, so this page says so plainly. What it offers instead is an easy find: no gate, no ticket, three veteran trees in one small forest clearing.
meta_description: Three legally protected trees, an oak and two limes, standing together in state forest near Toruń, all designated in one 2014 resolution.
question_meta: Brzoza has three protected trees, an oak and two limes standing together in state forest, none with a documented age.
question_answer: Brzoza has three protected trees and no documented age for any of them: the Gniewko Oak, measured at 375 to 415 centimetres round, and two limes at 380 and 320 centimetres, all made nature monuments together in 2014. The girths suggest centuries-old growth, but nobody has dated them.
question_context: All three trees stand within about fifteen metres of each other on one plot in section 178n of the Rudak forestry district, part of the Gniewkowo state forest district roughly ten kilometres north of Toruń. The Wielka Nieszawka municipal council made them nature monuments together in a single resolution, XLIII/207/2014, passed 7 October 2014 and gazetted later that month. The oak, named Dąb Gniewko, is given a girth of 375 centimetres by the forest district's own conservation page and 415 centimetres by Wikidata, plus a height of 26 metres in the second source; the two figures agree on species, place and designation date, so read the trunk as somewhere between them. The two limes, named Lipa Bolka and Lipa Brata Alberta after Brother Albert Chmielowski, measure 380 and 320 centimetres and rest on the forest district's page alone, which is why both are flagged. Nobody has dated any of the three. The setting is working state forest rather than a park, open to walk on under Poland's general right of access, with no gate and no ticket.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Brzoza?
faq.a: Nobody knows. None of the three protected trees here carries a documented age; the oak, Dąb Gniewko, is the largest at 375 to 415 centimetres round.

faq.q: Why are there three trees on one page?
faq.a: All three, an oak and two limes, stand within about fifteen metres of each other and were made nature monuments together in a single 2014 council resolution.
Yes. The trees stand in working state forest open to walk on under Poland's general right of access, with no gate or ticket.
The trees stand in Brzoza, Gmina Wielka Nieszawka, roughly 10 kilometres north of Toruń city centre; there is no public transport stop at the site itself.

trees.story:
This oak became a legal nature monument on the same day and in the same document as the two limes standing fifteen metres away. The Wielka Nieszawka council protected all three in resolution XLIII/207/2014 of 7 October 2014, gazetted at the end of that month, on a single forest plot in section 178n of the Rudak forestry district, about ten kilometres north of Toruń.

Its waistline depends on who did the measuring. The state forest district's own conservation page, quoting the council resolution, gives 375 centimetres. Wikidata gives 415, and adds a height of 26 metres. The two agree on species, place and designation date, so read the trunk as somewhere in that range rather than as either figure exactly.

Nobody has dated it. Polish nature-monument registers rarely carry an age, and girth on its own is a thin basis for ageing an oak when no source has done the calculation. If you know how old this one is, tell us.

The setting is working state forest rather than a park: Lasy Panstwowe ground, open to walk on under Poland's general right of access, with no gate and no ticket. That is much of the appeal. Nothing here has been laid out to show the trees off, and the three trunks stand close enough together that the whole protected group fits in one view once you have found the turning.

trees.story:
A lime rarely out-measures the oak growing fifteen metres away. On the forest district's own figures this one does, 380 centimetres round against the oak's 375. Both trees, along with a second lime, were made nature monuments together by the Wielka Nieszawka council in resolution XLIII/207/2014 of 7 October 2014, on one plot in section 178n of the Rudak forestry district north of Toruń.

Only one source carries this tree at all: the Gniewkowo forest district's conservation page, quoting that resolution. It gives the species, the girth and the plot, and stops there. No second register, no local write-up, no age. That is why this entry is flagged. Everything above rests on a single document, and a small-leaved lime approaching four metres round is old enough that somebody ought to have written more.

Small-leaved lime is the tree Polish villages plant on greens and along manor drives, for the shade and for the noise the bees make in it in July. This one grew up in working state forest instead, on Lasy Panstwowe ground you can walk on to under Poland's general right of access, ten kilometres from the middle of Toruń. No gate, no ticket, no path built for it. If you get a tape measure round it, or find a date for it anywhere, we would like to hear.

trees.story:
Somebody in the forest service named this lime after a saint. It stands on the register as Lipa Brata Alberta, the Brother Albert Lime, for St Brother Albert Chmielowski, and it is the smallest of three protected trees on one plot in section 178n of the Rudak forestry district: 320 centimetres round, against the neighbouring lime's 380 and the oak's 375. All three were made nature monuments in a single resolution of the Wielka Nieszawka council on 7 October 2014.

One source carries it, the Gniewkowo forest district's own conservation page, citing that resolution. It gives species, girth and plot and nothing else, which is why this entry is flagged. Nobody has recorded an age either, and 320 centimetres of small-leaved lime says the tree is old without saying how old. If you have seen a date for it anywhere, we would like to know.

The three trunks stand within about fifteen metres of each other in ordinary working state forest ten kilometres north of Toruń. There is no gate, no ticket and nothing laid on for visitors: Lasy Panstwowe ground, open to walk under Poland's general right of access. The reward for finding the turning is a group rather than a single tree, an oak and two limes protected in one sentence of municipal law and left otherwise entirely alone.
